questions.q: How is software engineering defined?
o: The process of writing computer programs for personal use
An engineering discipline concerned with all aspects of software production, from the early stages of system specification through to maintaining the system after it has gone into use
The study of computer hardware design
The marketing and sale of software products
questions.e: Software engineering is an engineering discipline concerned with all aspects of software production, from the early stages of system specification through to maintaining the system after it has gone into use — not just the technical process of development but also project management and supporting tools and methods.

questions.q: During the 'software development crisis', projects were characterised how?
o: Early, under budget, and highly reliable
Late, over budget, unreliable, difficult to maintain, and performing poorly
Small, simple, and always successful
Fully automated with no human effort
questions.e: The software development crisis referred to projects that were late, over budget, unreliable, difficult to maintain, and that performed poorly, which motivated a disciplined engineering approach.

questions.q: The Ariane 5 explosion, cited as a software crisis example, was caused by what?
o: A network intrusion by hackers
An overflow error — trying to store a 64-bit number into a 16-bit space — causing a crash after 36.7 seconds
A power failure at the launch site
A design flaw in the rocket engines
questions.e: The European Space Agency spent 10 years and $7 billion on Ariane 5, which crashed after 36.7 seconds; the crash was caused by an overflow error — trying to store a 64-bit number into a 16-bit space.

questions.q: What are the two types of software products?
o: Free products and paid products
Generic products (marketed to any customer) and customized/bespoke products (commissioned by a specific customer)
Hardware products and firmware products
Batch products and interactive products
questions.e: There are two types of software products: generic products, which are stand-alone systems marketed and sold to any customer (e.g. graphics programs), and customized (bespoke) products, which are commissioned by a specific customer to meet their own needs.

questions.q: For generic and customized software products respectively, who owns the specification of what the software should do?
o: The customer owns both
The developer owns the generic product's specification; the customer owns the customized product's specification
The developer owns both
No one owns the specification
questions.e: For a generic product, the specification is owned by the software developer, who decides on changes; for a customized product, the specification is owned by the customer, who makes decisions on required changes.

questions.q: What are the four fundamental software engineering activities?
o: Coding, testing, debugging, and deploying
Software specification, software development, software validation, and software evolution
Planning, organizing, staffing, and directing
Requirements, design, implementation, and installation
questions.e: The four fundamental software engineering activities are software specification (defining what the system should do), software development, software validation (checking it meets requirements), and software evolution (modifying it in response to change).

questions.q: What is the difference between software engineering and computer science?
o: They are identical
Computer science focuses on theory and fundamentals; software engineering is concerned with the practicalities of developing and delivering useful software
Computer science is about practicalities; software engineering is about theory
Software engineering does not involve computers
questions.e: Computer science focuses on theory and fundamentals, whereas software engineering is concerned with the practicalities of developing and delivering useful software.

questions.q: How is software defined?
o: Only the executable machine code
Computer programs and their associated documentation
The physical media on which programs are stored
The hardware that runs programs
questions.e: Software is computer programs and associated documentation (including system documentation and user documentation); software products may be developed for a particular customer or for a general market.

questions.q: Roughly how are software costs distributed between development and testing, and what is noted about custom software?
o: 90% development, 10% testing; evolution is free
Roughly 60% development costs and 40% testing costs; for custom software, evolution costs often exceed development costs
50% each; evolution never occurs
100% development; testing is unnecessary
questions.e: Roughly 60% of software costs are development costs and 40% are testing costs; for custom software, evolution (change after delivery) costs often exceed the original development costs.

questions.q: The non-functional attributes of good software describe quality. Which set lists key product characteristics?
o: Speed, colour, size, and weight
Maintainability, Dependability, Efficiency, and Usability
Specification, development, validation, and evolution
Planning, design, coding, and testing
questions.e: Key non-functional product characteristics of good software are Maintainability (testability, extensibility), Dependability (reliability, security, safety), Efficiency (response time, memory use), and Usability (easy and satisfying to use).

questions.q: Which application type is described as being numerically more common than any other type of system?
o: Stand-alone applications
Embedded control systems
Entertainment systems
Batch processing systems
questions.e: Embedded control systems — software systems that control and manage hardware devices — are numerically probably more common than any other type of system.

questions.q: The three key challenges facing software engineering are which of the following?
o: Speed, cost, and size
Heterogeneity, Delivery, and Trust
Specification, development, and validation
Planning, coding, and testing
questions.e: The three key challenges are heterogeneity (coping with diverse platforms and systems), delivery (delivering software in shorter times without compromising quality), and trust (demonstrating that software can be trusted by users).

questions.q: According to the practitioner's myths, what portion of all effort on software is expended AFTER it is first delivered?
o: Less than 10%
Between 60% and 80%
Exactly 40%
None; the job is done after delivery
questions.e: Contrary to the myth that the job is done once the program works, industry data indicate that between 60% and 80% of all effort expended on software is expended after it is first delivered to the customer (evolution and maintenance).

questions.q: What is a software process?
o: A single program that automates development
A set of activities and associated results that produce a software product (specification, development, validation, evolution)
The hardware used to run software
A contract between customer and developer
questions.e: A software process is a set of activities and associated results that produce a software product; the activities include specification (what the customer needs), development (design and programming), validation (checking requirements), and evolution (modifications).

questions.q: According to the management myth about schedules, what is the reality of adding more programmers to a late project?
o: It always allows the project to catch up quickly
Software development is not a mechanistic process; adding new people means existing staff must spend time educating newcomers, reducing productive effort
It has no effect on the schedule
It is the recommended solution to any delay
questions.e: The reality is that software development is not a mechanistic process like manufacturing; as new people are added, those already working must spend time educating the newcomers, thereby reducing productive development effort — people can be added but only in a well-coordinated manner.

questions.q: What is the difference between plan-driven and agile processes?
o: Plan-driven processes have no plan; agile processes plan everything upfront

In plan-driven processes all activities are planned in advance and progress is measured against the plan; in agile processes planning is incremental and easier to change to reflect changing requirements
They are identical
Agile processes cannot handle change
questions.e: In plan-driven processes all process activities are planned in advance and progress is measured against this plan; in agile processes planning is incremental and it is easier to change the process to reflect changing customer requirements. In practice most processes mix both, and there are no right or wrong software processes.

questions.q: In the six stages of the SDLC, which document is produced at the 'Defining Requirements' stage?
o: The DDS (Design Document Specification)
The SRS (Software Requirement Specification)
The UAT (User Acceptance Testing) report
The Gantt chart
questions.e: At the Defining Requirements stage, the product requirements are documented and approved through the SRS — the Software Requirement Specification — which consists of all product requirements to be designed and developed during the project life cycle.

questions.q: What is produced at the SDLC 'Designing the product architecture' stage, based on the SRS?
o: The SRS itself
The DDS (Design Document Specification), which documents the proposed design approaches
The source code
The deployment package
questions.e: Based on the requirements in the SRS, one or more design approaches for the product architecture are proposed and documented in the DDS (Design Document Specification), which is then reviewed by stakeholders to select the best design.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of the Waterfall model?
o: Phases overlap and are revisited freely
It was the first process model introduced; each phase must be completed before the next begins, with no overlapping of phases
It emphasises risk analysis in a spiral
It builds the system as a series of increments
questions.e: The Waterfall Model was the first process model introduced; in it, each phase must be completed before the next phase can begin, and there is no overlapping of the phases.

questions.q: When is the Waterfall model most appropriate?
o: When requirements are unclear and change frequently
When requirements are very well known, the product definition is stable, and the technology is understood (e.g. a new version or a port of an existing product)
For high-risk, complex projects
When frequent prototypes are needed
questions.e: The Waterfall model is appropriate when requirements are very well known and stable, the product definition is stable, the technology is understood, or when developing a new version of an existing product or porting a product to a new platform.

questions.q: What is throw-away prototyping used for?
o: Delivering the final production system
Deriving end-system requirements and reducing requirements risk; the prototype (e.g. screen mock-ups, storyboards) is discarded after use
Replacing testing entirely
Managing project schedules
questions.e: Throw-away prototyping is used to derive end-system requirements and reduce requirements risk; an initial prototype (such as screen mock-ups or storyboards) is developed from outline requirements, experimented with, and then discarded once the risk is acceptably low.

questions.q: How does the incremental model develop a system?
o: All at once in a single delivery

As a series of versions (increments), each adding functionality; requirements are divided into modules developed separately (each following the waterfall model) and integrated, with each module a standalone deliverable
Purely through prototypes that are thrown away
By assembling only off-the-shelf components
questions.e: In the incremental model the system is developed as a series of versions (increments), each adding functionality to the previous; requirements are divided into modules, each developed separately (following the waterfall model per module) and integrated, and each developed module is a standalone feature that can be delivered to users.

questions.q: Who introduced the Spiral model and in what year, and what does it emphasise?
o: Winston Royce, 1970; sequential phases
Barry Boehm, 1986; risk analysis, with the process represented as a spiral in which risks are explicitly assessed and resolved
Edsger Dijkstra, 1968; structured programming
Roger Pressman, 1992; component reuse
questions.e: The Spiral model was first mentioned by Barry Boehm in his 1986 paper; it is similar to the incremental model but places more emphasis on risk analysis, representing the process as a spiral in which risks are explicitly assessed and resolved throughout.

questions.q: The V-model is best described as which of the following?
o: A model with no testing phases
An extension of the waterfall model, also known as the Verification and Validation model, that associates a testing phase with each corresponding development stage in a V-shape
An agile, incremental model
A component-based development model
questions.e: The V-model is a sequential SDLC model executed in a V-shape, also known as the Verification and Validation model; it extends the waterfall model by associating a testing phase with each corresponding development stage.

questions.q: The Rational Unified Process (RUP) splits the project life cycle into which four phases?
o: Requirements, Design, Implementation, Maintenance
Inception, Elaboration, Construction, and Transition
Initiating, Planning, Executing, Closing
Specification, Development, Validation, Evolution
questions.e: RUP is an agile methodology that splits the project life cycle into four phases: Inception (defines scope, ~20% complete), Elaboration (plan, specify features, baseline architecture, ~80% complete), Construction (build the product in several iterations), and Transition (deploy the system).

questions.q: In the Rational Unified Process, the Inception and Elaboration phases are described as being roughly what percentage complete, respectively?
questions.e: In RUP, the Inception phase (which defines the scope) leaves the model about 20% complete, and after the Elaboration phase (planning, feature specification, and baselining the architecture) it is about 80% complete.

questions.q: What is component-based software engineering (CBSE)?
o: Building software entirely from the ground up
Building software from established software components (systematic reuse), where systems are integrated from existing components or COTS systems
A method of writing documentation
A testing technique
questions.e: Component-based software engineering (CBSE) is the idea of building software from established software components rather than from the ground up; it is based on systematic reuse, integrating systems from existing components or COTS (commercial-off-the-shelf) systems.

questions.q: What are the stated advantages and disadvantage of component-based software development?
o: Advantage: total control; disadvantage: high cost
Advantages: reducing cost and risk, and faster delivery; disadvantage: requirement compromises
Advantages: no reuse needed; disadvantage: slower delivery
There are no disadvantages
questions.e: The advantages of component-based development are reduced cost and risk and faster delivery of software; the main disadvantage is requirement compromises, since the system must be built around what the existing components can do.

questions.q: What are the two main ways of coping with change during a software process?
o: Adding programmers and outsourcing
System prototyping and incremental delivery
Waterfall and V-model
Documentation and testing
questions.e: The two main ways of coping with change are system prototyping (building a working model to reduce requirements risk) and incremental delivery (delivering the system in increments).

questions.q: What is a software requirement?
o: A description of how the software will be coded internally
A complete description of what the software system will do without describing how it will do it — a complete specification of the desired external behavior
A schedule for the project
The source code of the system
questions.e: A software requirement is a complete description of what the software system will do without describing how it will do it; it is a complete specification of the desired external behavior of the system (its response against the input).

questions.q: What is requirements engineering (RE)?
o: The process of writing source code
The process of finding out, analyzing, documenting, and checking the services the customer requires and the constraints on the system's operation
The process of testing a finished system
The process of marketing software
questions.e: Requirements engineering (RE) is the process of finding out, analyzing, documenting, and checking the services that the customer requires and the constraints on its operation; the artifact that comes out of the process is the SRS document.

questions.q: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
o: Functional requirements describe how the system works; non-functional describe what it does

Functional requirements are statements of services the system should provide (what it should do); non-functional requirements are constraints on those services (how it works/behaves, such as timing, standards, and development-process constraints)
They are identical
Functional requirements apply only to hardware
questions.e: Functional requirements are statements of the services the system should provide and how it should react to inputs — what the system should do. Non-functional requirements are constraints on the services or functions, such as timing constraints, standards, and development-process constraints — how the system works or behaves.

questions.q: What is the difference between user requirements and system requirements?
o: User requirements are code; system requirements are diagrams

User requirements are statements in natural language (plus diagrams) of the services and constraints, written from the users' perspective; system requirements are a structured document of detailed descriptions written from the developers' perspective, defining what should be implemented
They are the same document
System requirements are written before the project begins
questions.e: User requirements are statements in natural language plus diagrams of the services the system provides and its operational constraints, written from the users' perspective; system requirements are a structured document setting out detailed descriptions of the system's functions and constraints, written from the developers' perspective and defining what should be implemented.

questions.q: What are the process activities of requirements engineering?
o: Coding, testing, debugging, and releasing
Requirements elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, and management
Planning, organizing, staffing, and directing
Inception, elaboration, construction, and transition
questions.e: The RE process activities are requirements elicitation (discovering requirements from stakeholders), analysis (reasoning about them, resolving conflicts), specification (recording them), validation (confirming they are valid and complete), and management (managing all RE activities).

questions.q: What is requirements elicitation?
o: The final approval of requirements by the customer
The process through which customers, buyers, or users discover, reveal, articulate, and understand their requirements, involving technical staff working with stakeholders
The process of coding the requirements
The process of testing the system
questions.e: Requirements elicitation is the process through which the customers, buyers, or users of a software system discover, reveal, articulate, and understand their requirements; it involves technical staff working with stakeholders (end-users, managers, domain experts, etc.) to learn about the application domain, services, and constraints.

questions.q: Which of the following is a stated problem of requirements elicitation?
o: Stakeholders always know exactly what they want
Stakeholders may not know what they really want, may express requirements in their own terms, and different stakeholders may have conflicting requirements
Requirements never change
There is only ever one stakeholder
questions.e: Problems of requirements elicitation include: stakeholders don't know what they really want; they express requirements in their own terms; different stakeholders may have conflicting requirements; organizational and political factors may influence requirements; and requirements change during analysis as new stakeholders emerge.

questions.q: What does it mean for requirements to be complete and consistent?
o: Complete means short; consistent means long
Complete means they include descriptions of all required facilities; consistent means there are no conflicts or contradictions in the descriptions of the system facilities
They are the same property
Complete means tested; consistent means deployed
questions.e: In principle, requirements should be both complete — including descriptions of all facilities required — and consistent — having no conflicts or contradictions in the descriptions of the system facilities.

questions.q: According to IEEE Std 729, a requirement is a condition or capability that must be met by a system to satisfy what?
o: Only the developer's preferences
A contract, standard, specification, or other formally imposed document; it can be a constraint or functionality
Only the schedule
Only the budget
questions.e: Per IEEE Std 729, a requirement is a condition or capability that must be met or possessed by a system to satisfy a contract, standard, specification, or other formally imposed document; it can be a constraint or functionality.

questions.q: How are non-functional requirements classified?
o: Small, medium, and large requirements
Product requirements, organisational requirements, and external requirements
Functional, structural, and behavioral requirements
User, system, and business requirements
questions.e: Non-functional requirements are classified as product requirements (specifying how the delivered product must behave, e.g. execution speed, reliability), organisational requirements (consequences of organisational policies, e.g. process standards), and external requirements (arising from external factors, e.g. interoperability or legislative requirements).

questions.q: What problem does requirements imprecision cause, illustrated by the term 'search'?
o: It makes the system faster
Ambiguous requirements may be interpreted in different ways by developers and users (e.g. 'search' meaning search across all clinics versus search within one clinic)
It has no effect on the system
It only affects non-functional requirements
questions.e: When functional requirements are not precisely stated, ambiguous requirements may be interpreted differently by developers and users; for example, the term 'search' could mean searching for a patient name across all clinics (user intention) or within an individual clinic (developer interpretation).

questions.q: What is system modeling?
o: The process of writing source code
The process of developing abstract models of a system, with each model presenting a different view or perspective, usually using a graphical notation based on the UML
The physical construction of hardware
The testing of a completed system
questions.e: System modeling is the process of developing abstract models of a system, with each model presenting a different view or perspective of that system; it now usually means representing a system using a graphical notation based on the Unified Modeling Language (UML).

questions.q: The four perspectives from which a system may be modeled are which of the following?
o: Fast, slow, cheap, and expensive
External, structural, interaction, and behavioral perspectives
User, system, business, and technical perspectives
Past, present, future, and hypothetical
questions.e: A system may be modeled from an external perspective (context/environment), a structural perspective (organization or data structure), an interaction perspective (interactions between the system and its environment or components), and a behavioral perspective (dynamic behavior and response to events).

questions.q: In the UML, class diagrams and object diagrams are which category of diagram, and use case and activity diagrams are which?
o: Both are interaction diagrams
Class and object diagrams are structural; use case and activity diagrams are behavioral
Class diagrams are behavioral; use case diagrams are structural
All are structural diagrams
questions.e: In UML, structural diagrams (element of specification irrespective of time) include class, component, deployment, object, and package diagrams; behavioral diagrams (behavioral features of a system) include activity, state machine, and use case diagrams; interaction diagrams include sequence and communication diagrams.

questions.q: What is an object in object-oriented modeling?
o: A description of a group of similar things
A concept, abstraction, or thing with sharp boundaries and meaning for an application, having state, behavior, and identity
A relationship between two classes
A method that performs a calculation
questions.e: An object is a concept, abstraction, or thing with sharp boundaries and meaning for an application; it has state, behavior, and identity, and is represented as a rectangle with an underlined name. An object is an instance of a class.

questions.q: What is a class, and how is it represented in a class diagram?
o: A single object; a plain rectangle
A description of a group of objects with common attributes, operations, relationships, and semantics; represented as a compartmented rectangle with three sections (name, attributes, operations)
A relationship; a diamond
An actor; a stick figure
questions.e: A class is a description of a group of objects with common properties (attributes), behavior (operations), relationships, and semantics; an object is an instance of a class. A class is represented as a compartmented rectangle with three sections: the class name, the attributes, and the operations.

questions.q: What is an association relationship in a class diagram?
o: A whole-part relationship between an aggregate and its parts
A link between classes indicating that there is some relationship (a semantic connection) between them, so they can communicate
A relationship where one class inherits from another
A dependency where a change in one causes a change in another
questions.e: An association denotes a link between classes that indicates there is some relationship between them; if two classes need to communicate, there must be a link, and an association models this semantic connection (a family of links).

questions.q: What is the difference between aggregation and composition?
o: Aggregation is stronger ownership than composition
Aggregation is a whole-part ('has a') relationship, while composition is a stronger variant ('owns a') with strong ownership; composition is more specific than aggregation
They are identical
Composition is an inheritance relationship
questions.e: Aggregation is a special form of association modeling a whole-part ('has a') relationship between an aggregate (the whole) and its parts; composition is a stronger variant ('owns a') with strong ownership, and is more specific than aggregation.

questions.q: What is a generalization relationship in a class diagram?
o: A 'has a' whole-part relationship

A relationship where one class (subclass) shares the structure and/or behavior of one or more classes (superclasses), defining an 'is-a-kind-of' hierarchy in which the subclass inherits attributes, operations, and relationships
A 'using' relationship where a change in one class affects another
A link so two classes can communicate
questions.e: Generalization is a relationship among classes where one class (a subclass) shares the structure and/or behavior of one or more superclasses; it defines an 'is-a-kind-of' hierarchy in which the subclass inherits the parent's attributes, operations, and relationships, and may add its own. It supports single and multiple inheritance.

questions.q: What is a dependency relationship?
o: A whole-part relationship
A relationship between two model elements where a change in one may cause a change in the other — a 'using' relationship
An inheritance relationship
A multiplicity constraint
questions.e: A dependency is a relationship between two model elements where a change in one may cause a change in the other; it presents a 'using' relationship (e.g. a client depends on a supplier class).

questions.q: What does multiplicity specify in an association?
o: The order in which operations are called
How many objects participate in the relationship — the number of instances of one class related to one instance of the other class, specified at each end of the association
The direction of navigation only
The name of the association
questions.e: Multiplicity defines how many objects participate in a relationship — the number of instances of one class related to one instance of the other class — and is specified for each end of the association (e.g. 1, *, 0..1, 1..*, 0..*).

questions.q: In a generalization, what does a subclass inherit from its superclass?
o: Only the superclass's name
The parent's attributes, operations, and relationships (and it may add additional ones of its own)
Nothing; it starts fresh
Only the attributes, never the operations
questions.e: A subclass inherits its parent's attributes, operations, and relationships; the subclass may also add additional attributes, operations, and relationships of its own.

questions.q: What is an aggregation model used to show?
o: The dynamic behavior of a system over time
How classes that are collections are composed of other classes (similar to the part-of relationship in semantic data models)
The sequence of messages between objects
The states a system can occupy
questions.e: An object class aggregation model shows how classes that are collections are composed of other classes; aggregation models are similar to the part-of relationship in semantic data models.

questions.q: What do use case diagrams show, and whose perspective do they provide?
o: The internal code structure; the developer's perspective
The various activities that users can perform on the system, modeling the dynamic aspects and providing a user's perspective of the system
The sequence of messages over time; the tester's perspective
The data structure; the database administrator's perspective
questions.e: Use case diagrams show the various activities that users can perform on the system; they model the dynamic aspects of the system and provide a user's perspective. Use cases were originally developed to support requirements elicitation and are now part of UML.

questions.q: In a use case diagram, what is an actor and how is it represented?
o: An activity the user performs; represented by an ellipse
A user of the system playing a particular role (which may be a person or another system); represented by a stick figure
A relationship between use cases; represented by a line
The system boundary; represented by a rectangle
questions.e: An actor is a user of the system playing a particular role, representing something that uses the system (a person or another system); it is shown with a stick figure.

questions.q: How is a use case represented in a use case diagram?
o: By a stick figure
By an ellipse
By a rectangle
By a diamond
questions.e: A use case is a particular activity a user can do on the system and is represented by an ellipse. Actors are stick figures, and relationships are shown by lines connecting actors to use cases.

questions.q: What is the 'include' relationship between use cases?
o: A relationship where the included use case is optional
A relationship where a base use case is dependent on the included use case(s) — without them the base use case is incomplete, as the included use case(s) represent sub-sequences of the interaction
A relationship where a child inherits from a parent
A relationship connecting two actors
questions.e: In the include (inclusion) relationship, a base use case is dependent on the included use case(s); without them the base use case is incomplete, because the included use case(s) represent sub-sequences of the interaction that always occur.

questions.q: What is the 'extend' relationship between use cases?
o: A relationship where the base use case is always incomplete without it
A relationship used when a use case conditionally adds steps to another use case; the extending use case represents optional (should/could/want) behavior
An inheritance relationship between actors
A simple communication link
questions.e: The extend relationship is used when a use case conditionally adds steps to another first-class use case; the extending use case represents optional behavior (should/could/want), which is where the term 'optional' is relevant. This distinguishes it from include, where the included behavior is required.

questions.q: The generalization relationship among use cases (or actors) does what?
o: Makes the base use case incomplete
Allows child use cases (or specialized actors) to inherit behavior from parent use cases (or generalized actors)
Adds optional steps conditionally
Connects an actor to the system boundary
questions.e: Generalization allows child use cases to inherit behavior from parent use cases; similarly, an actor-to-actor generalization lets a specialized actor inherit from a generalized actor (e.g. Mom Cook and Father Cook specializing a generalized Cook actor).

questions.q: Which two UML diagrams are named for interaction modeling?
o: Class diagrams and object diagrams
Use case diagrams and sequence diagrams
Activity diagrams and state machine diagrams
ER diagrams and EER diagrams
questions.e: Use case diagrams and sequence diagrams may be used for interaction modeling; modeling user interaction helps identify user requirements, and modeling system-to-system interaction highlights potential communication problems.

questions.q: In use case terminology, what is the essential difference between 'include' and 'extend'?
o: Include is optional; extend is mandatory
Include represents required sub-sequences without which the base use case is incomplete, whereas extend conditionally adds optional steps to a use case
They are identical
Include connects actors; extend connects use cases
questions.e: Include represents required sub-sequences of interaction — without them the base use case is incomplete; extend conditionally adds optional steps (should/could/want behavior) to a first-class use case.

questions.q: What does an activity diagram describe, and what is it essentially?
o: The static structure of classes; a class hierarchy

How activities are coordinated and the dependencies between them (what can happen in parallel, what must finish before something else starts); it is essentially a flowchart showing the flow of control from activity to activity, representing the workflow of a process
The sequence of messages between objects over time
The data model of an organization
questions.e: An activity diagram describes how activities are coordinated, recording the dependencies between activities such as which things can happen in parallel and what must be finished before something else can start; it is essentially a flowchart showing the flow of control from activity to activity and represents the workflow of the process.

questions.q: What is the purpose of activity diagrams?
o: To show the physical deployment of hardware
To model business workflows and to model operations
To define the data structure of a database
To list project tasks against a calendar
questions.e: The purpose of activity diagrams is to model business workflows and to model operations; they commonly contain activity states, transitions, and objects.

questions.q: What is the function of a fork node and a join node in an activity diagram?
o: A fork ends the diagram; a join starts it

A fork node splits a single incoming flow into multiple concurrent flows, and a join node joins multiple concurrent flows back into a single outgoing flow; used together they are called synchronization
A fork is a decision; a join is a merge of alternatives
They both represent the start marker
questions.e: A fork node splits a single incoming flow into multiple concurrent flows (represented as a slightly thicker straight line), and a join node joins multiple concurrent flows back into a single outgoing flow; a fork and join used together are often referred to as synchronization.

questions.q: What are swimlanes in an activity diagram used for?
o: To represent decision points
To group related activities into columns, adding the dimension of visualizing roles — each swimlane shows the name of a role at the top and presents that role's activities
To split a flow into concurrent paths
To mark the start and stop of the diagram
questions.e: Swimlanes group related activities into one column, adding the dimension of visualizing roles; the diagram is separated into parallel segments called swimlanes, each showing the name of a role at the top and the activities of that role, with transitions able to move from one swimlane to another.

questions.q: In an activity diagram, what does a decision diamond represent?
o: The start of the workflow
A branch point where the flow follows different paths depending on a guard condition (e.g. [x>0], [x=0], [x<0])
Two concurrent flows merging
An object being created
questions.e: A decision diamond represents a branch point in an activity diagram where the flow follows different paths depending on guard conditions (such as [x>0], [x=0], [x<0]).

questions.q: Which elements does an activity diagram commonly contain?
o: Classes, attributes, and operations
Activity states, transitions, and objects
Entities, attributes, and relationships
Actors, use cases, and system boundaries
questions.e: Activity diagrams commonly contain activity states, transitions, and objects; notations include activities, transitions, start and stop markers, decision diamonds, and fork/join (synchronization) bars.

questions.q: What does a sequence diagram model?
o: The static class structure of a system
The interactions between actors and objects within a system, showing object interactions arranged in time sequence during a particular use case
The data entities of an organization
The physical deployment of components
questions.e: A sequence diagram is a UML interaction diagram used to model the interactions between the actors and objects within a system; it shows the sequence of interactions during a particular use case, arranging object interactions in time sequence and showing how processes operate and in what order.

questions.q: In a sequence diagram, what do the two axes represent?
o: Both axes represent time
The horizontal axis shows which object/participant is acting, and the vertical axis represents time (going down means forward in time)
The horizontal axis is time; the vertical axis is objects
Both axes represent objects
questions.e: In a sequence diagram, the horizontal axis shows which object or participant is acting, and the vertical axis represents time — going down the diagram means moving forward in time.

questions.q: What is a lifeline in a sequence diagram?
o: A horizontal arrow representing a message
A dashed vertical line drawn from an object or actor at the top of the diagram, representing the object's existence over time
A white rectangle showing the object is active
A diamond showing a decision
questions.e: Objects and actors are listed along the top of the diagram, each with a dashed (dotted) vertical line drawn from it — the lifeline — representing the object's existence over time; interactions between objects are shown as annotated horizontal arrows.

questions.q: What is an activation in a sequence diagram?
o: The dashed line representing an object's life
The white rectangle on a lifeline indicating that an object is responding to (handling) a message, starting when the message is received and ending when handling is done
The X marking an object's deletion
A message an object sends to itself
questions.e: The white rectangles on a lifeline are called activations and indicate that an object is responding to a message; an activation starts when the message is received and ends when the object is done handling the message.

questions.q: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous messages in a sequence diagram?
o: Synchronous messages are optional; asynchronous are required

A synchronous message is used when the sender waits for the receiver to process the message and return before continuing; an asynchronous message is used when the caller does not wait for the receiver before sending other messages
They are identical
Synchronous messages go to the same object; asynchronous go to different objects
questions.e: A synchronous message is used when the sender waits for the receiver to process the message and return before carrying on with another message; an asynchronous message is used when the caller does not wait for the receiver to process and return before sending other messages to other objects.

questions.q: What is a reflexive message in a sequence diagram?
o: A message returned to the sender
A message an object sends to itself, indicated by a message arrow that starts and ends at the same lifeline
A message that deletes an object
A message between two different actors
questions.e: A reflexive message is when an object sends a message to itself; it is indicated with a message arrow that starts and ends at the same lifeline.

questions.q: The alternative and option sequence fragments model which logic, respectively?
o: Both model loops

The alternative fragment models 'if then else' logic (a choice between two or more message sequences); the option fragment models 'if then' logic (a sequence that occurs only under a certain condition)
The alternative models 'if then'; the option models a loop
Both model 'if then else' logic identically
questions.e: The alternative combination fragment is used when a choice must be made between two or more message sequences, modeling 'if then else' logic; the option fragment indicates a sequence that occurs only under a certain condition, modeling an 'if then' statement (it is not divided into multiple operands).

questions.q: What is the purpose of the loop fragment and the reference (ref) fragment in a sequence diagram?
o: The loop deletes objects; the ref creates them
The loop fragment represents a repetitive sequence (with a guard condition), and the reference fragment lets you reuse part of one sequence diagram in another to manage the size of large diagrams
They both model 'if then else' logic
The loop shows synchronous messages; the ref shows asynchronous ones
questions.e: The loop fragment is used to represent a repetitive sequence, with 'loop' in the name box and a guard condition; the reference (ref) fragment manages the size of large sequence diagrams by letting you reuse or reference part of one sequence diagram in another.

questions.q: How is the creation and deletion of an object shown in a sequence diagram?
o: Creation with an X; deletion with a lower position
An object created after the scenario starts appears lower than the others (creation), and an X at the bottom of an object's lifeline indicates its deletion
Both are shown with white rectangles
Creation and deletion cannot be shown
questions.e: For object lifetime, an object created after the start of the scenario appears lower than the others (creation), and an X at the bottom of an object's lifeline indicates its deletion.

questions.q: What is the Entity-Relationship (E-R) model?
o: A programming language for databases
A detailed, logical representation of the data for an organization, expressed in terms of entities, the relationships among them, and the attributes of both
A model of the physical hardware storing the data
A testing methodology
questions.e: The E-R model is a detailed, logical representation of the data for an organization or business area, understandable to both users and IT technologists; it is expressed in terms of entities, the relationships (associations) among those entities, and the attributes (properties) of both, and is usually drawn as an E-R diagram.

questions.q: What is the difference between a strong entity type and a weak entity type?
o: A strong entity depends on another; a weak entity is independent

A strong entity type (rectangle) exists independently and has a unique identifier; a weak entity type (double rectangle) depends for its existence on another entity type (its identifying owner) and has no meaning without it
They are identical
A strong entity has attributes; a weak entity has none
questions.e: A strong entity type (drawn as a rectangle) exists independently of other entity types and always has a unique identifier (e.g. EMPLOYEE); a weak entity type (double rectangle) depends for its existence on some other entity type — the identifying owner — and has no meaning in the ER diagram without it (e.g. DEPENDENT).

questions.q: How is a derived attribute represented, and what is it?
o: A double-lined ellipse; an attribute with many values
An ellipse with a dashed line; an attribute whose value can be calculated from related attribute values (e.g. Years_Employed from Date_Employed and today's date)
An underlined name; the key of the entity
A diamond; a relationship
questions.e: A derived attribute is one whose value can be calculated or derived from other related attribute values (e.g. Years_Employed derived from Date_Employed and today's date); it is signified by an ellipse with a dashed line. A multi-valued attribute is drawn with a double-lined ellipse.

questions.q: How is an identifier (key) attribute represented in an ER diagram, and what does it do?
o: A dashed ellipse; it is derived
It is underlined; it uniquely identifies individual instances of an entity type (e.g. Student_ID)
A double rectangle; it depends on another entity
A diamond; it is a relationship
questions.e: An identifier (key) attribute is an attribute or combination of attributes that uniquely identifies individual instances of an entity type (e.g. Student_ID); it is shown underlined. A composite identifier (e.g. Flight_ID = Flight_Number + Date) is underlined while its components are not.

questions.q: What is the degree of a relationship, and what are the three most common degrees?
o: The number of attributes; simple, composite, derived
The number of entity types that participate in it; the three most common are unary (degree 1), binary (degree 2), and ternary (degree 3)
The number of instances; one, many, all
The strength of the relationship; weak, medium, strong
questions.e: The degree of a relationship is the number of entity types that participate in it; the three most common degrees are unary (degree 1, a recursive relationship between instances of one entity type), binary (degree 2, the most common), and ternary (degree 3).

questions.q: A unary relationship is which of the following?
o: A relationship between three entity types
A relationship between the instances of a single entity type (also called a recursive relationship), such as 'Manages' among EMPLOYEE instances
The most common type of relationship
A relationship with a single attribute
questions.e: A unary relationship is between the instances of a single entity type and is also called a recursive relationship; for example, 'Is_Married_To' is a one-to-one unary relationship among PERSON instances and 'Manages' is a one-to-many unary relationship among EMPLOYEE instances.

questions.q: What is a cardinality constraint, and how is 'many' shown?
o: The degree of a relationship; shown by a diamond
The number of instances of one entity that can or must be associated with each instance of another entity; a maximum cardinality of 'many' is indicated by the crow's-foot symbol
The number of attributes; shown by an ellipse
The uniqueness of a key; shown by underlining
questions.e: A cardinality constraint specifies the number of instances of one entity that can or must be associated with each instance of another entity; the maximum cardinality of 'many' (an unspecified number greater than 1) is indicated by the crow's-foot symbol on the relationship line.

questions.q: What concepts does the EER (Enhanced/Extended ER) model add to the basic ER model?
o: Only tables and columns
The concepts of subclass and superclass (IS-A), specialization and generalization, and union types (categories)
Nothing new; it is identical to ER
Only cardinality constraints
questions.e: The EER model includes all the concepts of the ER model and adds the concepts of a subclass and superclass (IS-A), specialization and generalization, and the concept of a union type or category (representing the union of objects of different entity types).

questions.q: What is the difference between specialization and generalization in the EER model?
o: They are the same process

Specialization is the top-down process of defining a set of subclasses of a superclass based on distinguishing characteristics; generalization is the reverse bottom-up process of combining several classes with common features into a superclass
Specialization combines classes; generalization splits them
Specialization applies to attributes; generalization to relationships
questions.e: Specialization is the process of defining a set of subclasses of a superclass based on some distinguishing characteristic (top-down); generalization is the reverse process, in which several classes with common features are combined (generalized) into a superclass and the original classes become its subclasses (bottom-up), e.g. CAR and TRUCK generalized into VEHICLE.

questions.q: What do the disjointness constraints 'disjoint (d)' and 'overlapping (o)' specify in a specialization?
o: Disjoint means every entity is in a subclass; overlapping means none are
Disjoint (d) means an entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization; overlapping (o) means the same entity may be a member of more than one subclass
They are identical
Disjoint applies to attributes; overlapping to keys
questions.e: The disjointness constraint specifies whether subclasses are disjoint: 'disjoint' (d) means an entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization; 'overlapping' (o) means the same entity may be a member of more than one subclass.

questions.q: What do the completeness constraints 'total' and 'partial' specify in a specialization/generalization?
o: Total means an entity can avoid all subclasses; partial means it cannot
Total specifies that every entity in the superclass must be a member of some subclass (shown by a double line); partial allows an entity not to belong to any subclass (shown by a single line)
They are identical
Total applies to attributes; partial to relationships
questions.e: The completeness (exhaustiveness) constraint: 'total' specifies that every entity in the superclass must be a member of some subclass in the specialization/generalization (shown by a double line), while 'partial' allows an entity not to belong to any of the subclasses (shown by a single line). Combined with disjointness, this gives four types: disjoint total, disjoint partial, overlapping total, and overlapping partial.

questions.q: What is the difference between a specialization hierarchy and a specialization lattice?
o: A hierarchy allows multiple superclasses; a lattice allows only one

In a hierarchy every subclass has only one superclass (single inheritance, a tree structure); in a lattice a subclass can be a subclass of more than one superclass (multiple inheritance, a shared subclass)
They are identical
A hierarchy applies to attributes; a lattice to relationships
questions.e: In a specialization hierarchy, every subclass participates as a subclass in only one class/subclass relationship, so each subclass has only one superclass — single inheritance, resulting in a tree structure. In a specialization lattice, a subclass can be a subclass in more than one class/subclass relationship (multiple inheritance); a subclass with more than one superclass is called a shared subclass.

questions.q: What is an attribute, and to how many entities or relationships is it associated?
o: A relationship; associated with many entities
A property or characteristic of an entity type (drawn in an ellipse), associated with exactly one entity or relationship
A key that identifies instances; associated with none
A diamond linking two entities
questions.e: An attribute is a property or characteristic of an entity type (e.g. EMPLOYEE's Employee_Name); it is placed in an ellipse connected by a line to its associated entity, may also be associated with relationships, and is associated with exactly one entity or relationship.

questions.q: According to the PMI, what is a project?
o: A permanent, ongoing operation with no end date
A temporary endeavor (having specific start and completion dates) undertaken to create a unique product or service
Any repetitive manufacturing process
A software program that manages tasks
questions.e: According to the PMI definition, a project is a temporary endeavor (having specific start and completion dates) undertaken to create a unique product or service; 'temporary' means it has a definite beginning and end, and 'unique' means the product or service differs in some distinguishing way from all similar ones.

questions.q: What is project management?
o: Writing the source code for a project

The discipline of planning, organizing, and managing resources to bring about the successful completion of specific project goals — the art of maximizing the probability that a project delivers its goals on Time, within Budget, and at the required Quality
The testing of a finished product
The marketing of a product
questions.e: Project management is the discipline of planning, organizing, and managing resources to bring about the successful completion of specific project goals and objectives; it is the art of maximizing the probability that a project delivers its goals on Time, within Budget, and at the required Quality, by applying knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques.

questions.q: The PMBOK recognizes five basic process groups. Which set lists them?
o: Requirements, Design, Implementation, Testing, Maintenance
Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, and Closing
Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition, Deployment
Specification, Development, Validation, Evolution, Retirement
questions.e: The PMBOK (Project Management Body of Knowledge) recognizes five basic process groups: Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, and Closing.

questions.q: How many knowledge areas has the PMI suggested for project management?
o: Five
Seven
Nine
Twelve
questions.e: The PMI has suggested nine knowledge areas: Project Integration, Scope, Time, Cost, Quality, Human Resource, Communications, Risk, and Procurement Management.

questions.q: What is the difference between a PERT chart and a Gantt chart?
o: A PERT chart is a bar chart; a Gantt chart is a network model
A PERT chart is a graphical network model depicting the interdependencies between a project's tasks; a Gantt chart is a bar chart depicting project tasks against a calendar
They are identical
A PERT chart shows cost; a Gantt chart shows quality
questions.e: A PERT (Project Evaluation and Review Technique) chart is a graphical network model used to depict the interdependencies between a project's tasks; a Gantt chart is a bar chart used to depict project tasks against a calendar.

questions.q: What does PERT stand for, and what was it developed to make clear?
o: Project Estimation and Resource Tracking; the budget
Project Evaluation and Review Technique; the interdependence between project tasks before those tasks are scheduled
Program Execution and Review Timeline; the test results
Project Efficiency Rating Tool; the team's productivity
questions.e: PERT stands for Project Evaluation and Review Technique; it was developed to make clear the interdependence between project tasks before those tasks are scheduled. In a PERT chart, boxes represent tasks and arrows indicate that one task depends on the start or completion of another.

questions.q: What advantages make Gantt charts popular?
o: They hide overlapping tasks and are hard to read
They clearly show overlapping tasks (tasks performed at the same time), bars can be shaded to indicate percentage completion, and they are simple — easy to learn, read, prepare, and use
They automatically write the project's code
They eliminate the need for a schedule
questions.e: Gantt charts clearly show overlapping tasks (tasks that can be performed at the same time), their bars can be shaded to indicate percentage completion and progress, and their popularity stems from their simplicity — they are easy to learn, read, prepare, and use.

questions.q: What is the critical path in the Critical Path Method (CPM)?
o: The path with the shortest duration
The sequence of activities with the longest total duration; a delay in any of these activities will delay the whole project
The path with the fewest activities
The path that can be delayed without consequence
questions.e: In the Critical Path Method (CPM), the critical path is the sequence of activities with the longest duration; a delay in any of these activities will result in a delay for the whole project. CPM identifies which activities must finish on time and calculates the minimum time to complete the project.

questions.q: If a project's three possible paths have durations of 38 hours, 49 hours, and 41 hours, which is the critical path and what is the project's minimum duration?
o: The 38-hour path; 38 hours
The 49-hour path; 49 hours
The 41-hour path; 41 hours
The average of the three; 43 hours
questions.e: The critical path is the path with the longest total duration, so the 49-hour path is the critical path; because every path must complete, the minimum time to complete the whole project equals the critical path length, 49 hours.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists management activities in the project-management context?
o: Compiling, linking, executing, and debugging
Planning, Organizing, Staffing, Directing, Monitoring, Controlling, Innovating, and Representing
Specification, Development, Validation, and Evolution
Inception, Elaboration, Construction, and Transition
questions.e: Management involves the activities of Planning (deciding what is to be done), Organizing (making arrangements), Staffing (selecting the right people), Directing (giving instructions), Monitoring (checking progress), Controlling (remedying hold-ups), Innovating (new solutions), and Representing (communicating with users).

questions.q: What is software project management?
o: The management of hardware only
A sub-discipline of project management in which software projects are planned, monitored, and controlled
The writing of software documentation
The testing phase of the SDLC
questions.e: Software project management is a sub-discipline of project management in which software projects are planned, monitored, and controlled; because software development is a complex undertaking, especially with many people over a long time, such projects need to be managed.
